newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech IPB sees H1 profits cut in half.
newsitem.headline: Czech IPB sees H1 profits cut in half.

text.p: The third largest Czech bank, IPB a.s. said on Monday that after-tax profits in the first six months of the year slumped to almost half the levels posted in the same period in 1996.
IPB said in a statement that first half profits fell to 445 million crowns ($12.8 million), according to Czech accounting standards, from 830 million in the first six months last year.

It blamed the results on media speculation in April (later refuted) that the bank was in trouble, the arrest of the bank's general director on fraud charges, and the interest rate instability attending the recent assault on the crown.
Analysts said the results were lower than expected but likely to be the first in a line of poor profit figures from Czech banks.

"The earnings are quite a bit lower than last year and I think this is going to be quite a general thing for the banking sector this year because of the losses on the fixed income portfolio that the banks own and because of the economic slowdown," said ING Baring's Vojtech Kraus.
In the wake of a speculative attack on the Czech crown in May, the central bank raised interest rates sharply.
The Lombard rate was hiked to 50 percent from 14 perecnt, short term rates on the money markets surged to over 100 percent and the discount rate was moved up to 13.0 percent from 10.5.

"The economic situation of the bank...was affected by the unstable situation on the finanical markets in May and June which led to sharp rises in interest rates on deposits which it was not possible to fully cover on interest rates on credit," IPB's statement accompanying the results said.

ING Barings' Kraus said that the key question for equity investors interested in IPB was likely to be last week's announcement that Nomura Securities Co Ltd International would buy a 36 percent state-held stake in IPB.

The price was set at around six billion crowns but will not be finalised until an audit of the bank has taken place. The Finance Ministry also said that Nomura would raise IPB's basic capital by around six billion crowns.
"The key question for IPB really isn't this year's earnings but rather what happens when Nomura takes over particularly ...about increasing the share capital of IPB," he said.
"So the questions are how its going to be priced and what kind of diminution it's going to bring to the minority owners of the bank."
On Monday, IPB fell seven crowns, or 2.7 percent, to 255 on the Prague Stock Exchange after sharp gains on Thursday and Friday following the Nomura announcement.

Investors and international organisations have long been calling on the Czech government to push on with the privatisation of Czech banks which are generally perceived as lacking the competitive edge of foreign rivals.

The IPB sale was delayed by a Finance Ministry investigation into the bank's investment subsidiary, Prvni Investicni a.s. (PIAS) which resulted in a 10 million crown fine for for illegal financing operations and other violations.

In April, IPB posted a net profit, according to international accounting standards, of 882 million crowns ($29.2 million) saying its net profit fell from 1.01 billion crowns in 1995 mainly on the creation of reserves and provisions, as ordered by its auditor, Ernst & Young.
